blocks.text: You already know how rolling(window=3) works from the Window Functions lesson. Pandas builds a fixed size window covering exactly 3 rows, slides it forward one row at a time, and min_periods decides how strict it is about a window being completely full before it produces a result. None of that mechanic changes here. What changes is the question you are actually asking pandas to answer.

So far, window equal to 3 has meant exactly 3 rows, full stop, regardless of what dates those 3 rows actually landed on. But a huge amount of real world time series data does not arrive as one clean row per day. Sensors go offline for a while. Markets close on weekends and holidays. Logs get dropped. The moment your data has gaps or uneven spacing, counting rows and counting real calendar time stop meaning the same thing. That gap between the two is exactly what this lesson is about.

blocks.alt: A DatetimeIndex feeding a rolling 7D window which produces one smoothed value per row
blocks.caption: A time based window is anchored to real calendar time, not to a fixed count of rows.

blocks.text: 1. Introduction

This lesson assumes you already have the rolling window mental model down: what a window is, how it slides, and what min_periods does. None of that gets repeated here. Instead this lesson jumps straight into the one thing that changes once your index is made of real timestamps instead of plain row numbers, and it turns out to be a genuinely important change once your data has any gaps in it at all.

items: A temperature sensor that occasionally loses power for a few days and reports nothing during that stretch.
Stock prices that only exist on trading days, so weekends and holidays simply are not there.
Server logs where an outage means an entire block of expected entries never got written.
An app usage log where a user might open the app daily for a week, then not touch it again for ten days.

blocks.title: What this lesson is not re-covering
blocks.content: The sliding window idea, min_periods, and chaining aggregations like mean, sum, and std onto rolling are all covered in the Window Functions lesson earlier in this course. If any of that feels shaky, that is the lesson to revisit first. This one builds directly on top of it.

blocks.text: 1.1 Why Row Count and Calendar Time Are Not the Same Thing

Picture a rolling window of 3 rows sitting on data that is not evenly spaced. If your readings happen to land on three consecutive days, a 3 row window and a 3 day window describe the exact same thing. But that is a coincidence of your data being dense right there, not a guarantee window=3 gives you.

blocks.alt: A row based window of 3 rows straddling a gap and ending up spanning 19 real calendar days
blocks.caption: Three rows is always three rows, but the real time those three rows span depends entirely on what happened to be recorded.

blocks.text: If your third row happens to be recorded 19 days after the first one, because nothing got logged in between, your window of 3 rows for statistical purposes is now averaging together values that are 19 real days apart. Pandas has no idea that happened. It just sees 3 rows and does exactly what you told it to do: average the 3 rows. Whether those 3 rows represent 3 days or 3 weeks of real time is entirely invisible to a row based window.
1.2 The Fix: Pass a Time String Instead of an Integer

The fix is smaller than it sounds. Instead of passing an integer to window, you pass a time string, called an offset alias in pandas. Everything else about calling .rolling() stays exactly the same, you still chain an aggregation like .mean() or .std() onto it afterward.

code.content:
# what you already know: an integer means an exact row count
sales.rolling(window=3).mean()

# what is new here: a time string means a real calendar span
sensor.rolling('7D').mean()

blocks.alt: A 7D window always spanning from Jan 1 to Jan 7 regardless of whether that span holds 2 rows or 20 rows
blocks.caption: A time based window is defined by a real span of calendar time first. How many rows fall inside it is whatever your data happens to provide.

blocks.text: That single change, a string like '7D' instead of an integer like 3, tells pandas to stop counting rows entirely and instead build a window that always spans exactly 7 real calendar days, ending at the current row's timestamp. However many rows happen to fall inside that 7 day span, whether that is 1 row or 20, all of them get included. That is the entire idea this lesson is built around.
2. Time Based Windows Require a Real DatetimeIndex

A time based window only means something if pandas knows what time each row actually happened at. That is not optional here. Having a date column sitting in your DataFrame is not enough, the dates need to actually be the index, and that index needs to genuinely be a datetime type, not text that merely looks like a date.

code.content:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({
    "date": ["2024-01-01", "2024-01-02", "2024-01-03"],
    "reading": [21.2, 21.5, 20.9],
})

df["date"] = pd.to_datetime(df["date"])
df = df.set_index("date").sort_index()

df["reading"].rolling("7D").mean()

blocks.alt: A plain integer index causing rolling 7D to fail, next to a real DatetimeIndex letting it work
blocks.caption: Time based windows need a genuine DatetimeIndex. A date shaped column is not the same thing as a datetime shaped index.

blocks.title: Two gotchas pandas will actually tell you about
blocks.content: Try rolling('7D') on a plain integer index and pandas raises a clear error about the window needing to be an integer, since it has no notion of time to anchor a 7 day span to. Try it on a DatetimeIndex that is not sorted oldest to newest and pandas raises a clear error about the index needing to be monotonic. Both fail loudly rather than silently giving you a wrong answer, which is exactly what you want.

blocks.text: 2.1 Setting It Up in Practice

code.content:
df = pd.read_csv("sensor_log.csv", parse_dates=["date"])
df = df.set_index("date").sort_index()

# now every rolling call below can use a time string
df["reading"].rolling("7D").mean()
df["reading"].rolling("7D").std()

blocks.text: parse_dates handles the conversion to a real datetime type at load time, and sort_index() right after set_index() is worth making a habit of. A time based window assumes the timestamps are already in order, and getting that wrong is a much easier mistake to make than it sounds, especially after a merge or a concat from multiple sources.
2.2 Row Based Versus Time Based At a Glance
Put side by side, the two flavors of .rolling() answer genuinely different questions, even though the code looks almost identical.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Aspect","rolling(window=3)","rolling('7D')"],"rows":[["What it counts","Exactly 3 rows, every single time","Every row whose timestamp falls within the trailing 7 calendar days"],["Span on evenly spaced daily data","Always exactly 3 days","Always exactly 7 days"],["Span on irregular data with gaps","Can stretch across anywhere from a couple of days to several weeks, purely by accident of where the gaps land","Always exactly 7 calendar days, no matter how many rows land inside it"],["Number of rows inside the window","Always exactly 3","Varies. Could be 1 row, could be 20, depending on how densely packed your data is"],["What you pass to window","An integer","A time string, like 7D, 30D, or 24H"]]}

blocks.title: The default min_periods quietly changes too
blocks.content: Row based rolling defaults to requiring a completely full window before producing a result, which is why the first couple of rows come back as NaN. Time based rolling defaults to min_periods=1 instead, so it will happily give you an answer from just one row if that is all that has happened in the last 7 days so far. That is convenient, but it also means an early or sparse rolling value might be based on far less data than the window size suggests, so do not assume every value in a time based rolling column carries equal statistical weight.

blocks.text: 3. Common Time Window Strings
The strings you pass to a time based window are called offset aliases, and in practice you will reach for a small handful of them over and over.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Window string","Meaning","Typical use"],"rows":[["7D","A trailing 7 calendar day window","A weekly rolling average or weekly rolling volatility"],["30D","A trailing 30 calendar day window, roughly a month","A rough monthly trend line"],["24H","A trailing 24 hour window","A daily rolling average computed on hourly or sub daily sensor data"],["1H","A trailing 1 hour window","Smoothing very high frequency sensor or tick data"],["90D","A trailing 90 calendar day window, roughly a quarter","A quarterly rolling trend for slower moving metrics"]]}

blocks.alt: Three labeled boxes for 7D one week, 30D about one month, and 24H one day of hourly data
blocks.caption: The handful of time window strings you will actually reach for most often in practice.

blocks.title: 30D is not quite a calendar month
blocks.content: 30D always means exactly 30 times 24 hours, not the actual calendar month, which might be 28, 29, 30, or 31 days depending on which month it is. For most rolling average purposes that difference does not matter much, but it is worth knowing 30D is an approximation of a month rather than the real thing.

blocks.text: 3.1 Sub Daily Windows With Hours

When your data is more frequent than one row per day, like a sensor reporting every few minutes, the same idea works with hours instead of days. 24H gives you a genuine trailing 24 hour window, computed on whatever timestamps you actually have, even if readings arrive at irregular intervals throughout the day.
4. Worked Example: Rolling Average and Rolling Standard Deviation on Irregular Sensor Data

Let's make all of this concrete with a real, genuinely irregular dataset: a temperature sensor that goes offline for about a week, comes back online, and then reports one clearly anomalous reading a few days later.
4.1 Building the Irregular Dataset

blocks.alt: A timeline of sensor readings from Jan 1 to Jan 3, a gap with no data through Jan 10, then readings resuming on Jan 11
blocks.caption: A one week outage sits right in the middle of this sensor log, which is exactly the kind of irregularity a time based window needs to handle correctly.

blocks.text: Three readings, then a week long outage, then readings resume and run daily for a while, with one obviously odd value showing up on Jan 19. This is a small dataset on purpose, small enough that you can trace every single window by eye.
4.2 The 7 Day Rolling Average
Here is every row, alongside how many actual readings fell inside that row's trailing 7 day window and what the resulting average was.

blocks.alt: One week with only 3 readings producing an average of those 3 values, another week with 7 readings producing an average of all 7
blocks.caption: The 7D window always covers a real 7 day span, but it correctly adapts to however many readings actually exist inside each span.

blocks.text: Look at Jan 11, right after the outage ends. The window is still a genuine trailing 7 days, but only 1 reading actually exists inside that span, so the average is just that 1 reading. By Jan 17, a full week of dense daily data has accumulated inside the window, so the count climbs back up to 7. The window size in real time never changed. What changed is how much actual data pandas found inside it, and it handled that completely correctly without you doing anything special.

blocks.title: Confirmed here: min_periods defaults to 1 on time based windows
blocks.content: Jan 1 returns 21.20 immediately, using just that single reading, not NaN. That is the min_periods=1 default for time based rolling in action, and this dataset is a good concrete example of exactly when it matters: right after the outage, the rolling average is quietly based on very little data, even though it looks like a normal number in the table.

blocks.text: 4.3 Row Based Versus Time Based, Side by Side on the Same Gap
To see the actual practical damage a row based window can do here, compare how many real days a plain rolling(window=3) spans right around that same outage.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Date","Real days spanned by a row based window of 3","Real days spanned by a time based window of 7D"],"rows":[["Jan 3","2 days, Jan 1 through Jan 3","Always 7 days"],["Jan 11","9 days, jumping straight across the outage from Jan 3","Always 7 days"],["Jan 12","9 days, still straddling the outage","Always 7 days"],["Jan 13","Back down to 2 days once the gap has scrolled out","Always 7 days"]]}

blocks.text: Right at the boundary of the outage, the row based window of 3 silently stretches to cover 9 real days, quietly averaging together values from before and after a week long gap as if nothing happened. A moment later, once the gap has scrolled past, the same window drops right back down to spanning just 2 days. Nothing about your window size changed, only the accident of where the gap happened to fall. The time based window never has this problem. It stays anchored to a real 7 day span the entire time, whether the outage happens to land inside it or not.
4.4 The 7 Day Rolling Standard Deviation

blocks.alt: A 7D window of readings feeding a rolling standard deviation, branching into a low std meaning steady and a high std meaning volatile
blocks.caption: The same rolling mechanic, just a different aggregation: standard deviation instead of average, measuring how spread out the last 7 days actually were.

blocks.text: Through most of this dataset the rolling standard deviation sits quietly around 0.2 to 0.3, which makes sense, the sensor is reporting steady values in the low 20s day after day. Then Jan 19 comes in at 38.6, wildly out of line with everything around it, and the rolling standard deviation jumps to 6.29 and stays there for the next two rows, because that one anomalous reading is still sitting inside the trailing 7 day window each time.

blocks.alt: Normal readings keeping rolling std low, then a sudden odd reading making rolling std spike, flagged as worth investigating as an outlier
blocks.caption: A spike in rolling standard deviation is exactly the kind of signal worth watching for, and worth investigating further.

blocks.title: This connects directly to outlier detection
blocks.content: A rolling standard deviation that suddenly spikes is a genuinely useful, practical volatility or anomaly signal, not just a statistics exercise. It tells you the last 7 real days looked far less steady than usual, which is often the very first hint something unusual happened. The dedicated outlier detection lesson later in this course builds directly on this idea, using exactly this kind of rolling volatility signal to flag suspicious values automatically.

blocks.text: 5. Rolling Correlation and Rolling Covariance Between Two Columns

Everything so far has been one column at a time. Rolling windows work just as well between two columns, and this is where they become genuinely powerful for tracking a relationship, not just a single trend. A single correlation number computed across an entire dataset tells you how two things related on average over the whole period, and that single number can quietly hide a relationship that was strong for a while and then fell apart.
5.1 Rolling Correlation With rolling corr

Call .rolling() on one column as usual, then chain .corr() onto it and pass in the other column. Pandas recomputes the correlation fresh inside every window as it slides forward, instead of collapsing the whole dataset into one number.

blocks.alt: Stock A and stock B prices feeding both a single static correlation number and a rolling correlation over time, with the rolling version showing almost perfect correlation early on and much weaker correlation later
blocks.caption: A single static correlation number averages away exactly the kind of shift a rolling correlation catches as it happens.

blocks.text: Across this whole period, the static whole dataset correlation between these two stocks comes out to 0.73. That single number makes it sound like a moderately strong, fairly steady relationship the entire time. The rolling view tells a very different story: correlation was almost perfect, 0.98 and 0.99, for the first stretch, then dropped as low as 0.44 later on. Two stocks that used to move nearly in lockstep started drifting apart, and the static number completely buries that. Tracking rolling correlation like this is exactly how you would actually notice two assets decoupling in practice, rather than computing one number for the whole dataset and calling it done.
5.2 Rolling Covariance With rolling cov

Covariance measures the same kind of relationship as correlation, whether two columns tend to move together or move apart, but without normalizing it onto a fixed scale. Where correlation is always bounded between negative 1 and positive 1, covariance carries the actual units and scale of your data, so its raw magnitude is harder to compare across different pairs of columns.

blocks.alt: Two columns inside a rolling time window feeding rolling covariance, branching into positive meaning they move together and negative meaning they move apart
blocks.caption: Rolling covariance answers the same directional question as rolling correlation, just without the fixed scale.

blocks.title: When to reach for corr instead of cov
blocks.content: In practice, correlation is usually the one you reach for first, precisely because its bounded scale makes it easy to interpret and to compare across completely different pairs of columns. Covariance mainly earns its keep when you specifically need the unnormalized version, for instance as a direct input into a downstream calculation like a covariance matrix in portfolio risk analysis.

blocks.text: 6. Wrapping Up

Everything in this lesson comes down to one shift: letting a real span of calendar time define your window instead of a fixed count of rows. On clean, evenly spaced daily data the two approaches barely differ. The moment your data has gaps, which real world data almost always does eventually, a row based window quietly stretches and shrinks in real time span by accident, while a time based window stays anchored to exactly the span you asked for, no matter how sparse or dense the data inside it turns out to be.

items: Passing a time string like '7D' to rolling instead of an integer builds a window defined by real calendar time, not by row count.
Time based windows require a genuine DatetimeIndex, sorted oldest to newest, not just a date shaped column sitting somewhere in the DataFrame.
On irregular data, a row based window can silently stretch across far more real time than intended whenever it straddles a gap.
7D, 30D, and 24H cover a week, roughly a month, and a day of sub daily data, and are the offset aliases you will reach for most often.
Time based rolling defaults to min_periods=1, so an early or sparse window can produce a real looking number from very little actual data.
rolling().corr() and rolling().cov() track how a relationship between two columns changes over time, instead of collapsing it into one static number for the whole dataset.
A spike in rolling standard deviation is a genuinely practical volatility or anomaly signal, and it feeds directly into the outlier detection lesson coming up next in this course.

blocks.alt: A row based window of 3 spanning a variable number of days next to a time based window of 7D always spanning exactly 7 real days
blocks.caption: The whole lesson compressed into one contrast: a fixed row count that drifts in real time span, versus a fixed real time span that always stays exactly 7 days.

blocks.title: Where this connects next
blocks.content: The rolling standard deviation spike you saw in the worked example above is not just a one off curiosity. Watching for exactly that kind of spike is one of the core practical techniques the upcoming outlier detection lesson builds on, so keep that mental picture of a calm rolling std suddenly jumping handy, you are about to see it put to direct use.
